name: Continental Illinois

summary.text: Continental Illinois National Bank and Trust Company of Chicago was among the largest banks in the United States when it suffered a run on its wholesale funding in May 1984. The FDIC's own history describes its resolution as the largest in U.S. history to that point. On May 17, 1984 the FDIC, the Federal Reserve and the Comptroller of the Currency announced interim assistance under which depositors and other general creditors were to be fully protected; in July 1984 the FDIC took an 80 percent interest in the holding company. The episode is widely associated with the phrase 'too big to fail'.

sources.title: History of the Eighties, Vol. 1, Chapter 7: Continental Illinois and 'Too Big to Fail'
Continental Illinois: A Bank That Was Too Big to Fail

facts.claim: The FDIC's History of the Eighties describes the May 1984 Continental Illinois crisis as the largest bank resolution in U.S. history to that point, and says that the bank's size, as the nation's seventh-largest, forced regulators to recognize that very large institutions could fail.
facts.quote: The FDIC chapter opens by calling the May 1984 crisis the largest bank resolution in U.S. history, and says Continental, as the nation's seventh-largest bank, pushed regulators to recognize that very large institutions could fail.

sources.title: History of the Eighties, Vol. 1, Chapter 7: Continental Illinois and 'Too Big to Fail'
Continental Illinois and 'Too Big to Fail'

facts.claim: Continental had purchased about $1 billion in loan participations from Penn Square Bank of Oklahoma, which had generated billions of dollars of speculative oil and gas loans, many of them nearly worthless; after Penn Square failed in 1982, Continental's funding costs rose and it relied more on money-market sources such as the eurodollar market.
facts.quote: Penn Square had generated billions of dollars in extremely speculative oil and gas exploration loans, many of which were nearly worthless, and Continental had purchased a monumental $1 billion in participations from Penn Square.

sources.title: Continental Illinois: A Bank That Was Too Big to Fail

facts.claim: During the May 1984 run, depositors withdrew more than $6 billion in the week ending May 17, 1984; Federal Reserve History records that the bank lost about 30 percent of its funding over ten days and borrowed $3.6 billion from the Federal Reserve Bank of Chicago.
facts.quote: depositors withdrew more than $6 billion in a one-week period ending on May 17, 1984

sources.title: Can a Bank Run Be Stopped? Government Guarantees and the Run on Continental Illinois
Continental Illinois: A Bank That Was Too Big to Fail

facts.claim: On May 17, 1984 the FDIC, in a joint release with the Federal Reserve and the Comptroller of the Currency, announced interim assistance and gave assurance that in any permanent solution all depositors and other general creditors would be fully protected, regardless of the $100,000 deposit insurance limit.
facts.quote: depositors and other general creditors would be fully protected and service to customers would continue

sources.title: Statement on Federal Assistance to Continental Illinois Corporation and Continental Illinois National Bank, by William M. Isaac, Chairman
Can a Bank Run Be Stopped? Government Guarantees and the Run on Continental Illinois

facts.claim: In the permanent assistance plan of 1984 the FDIC infused $1 billion of capital, assumed the $3.5 billion the bank owed to the Federal Reserve Bank of Chicago, and took an 80 percent ownership interest in Continental's holding company; shareholders lost their investments and management was removed.
facts.quote: the FDIC taking 80 percent ownership in Continental's holding company and assuming responsibility for Continental's loan from the Federal Reserve. Shareholders lost their investments and management was removed.

sources.title: Continental Illinois: A Bank That Was Too Big to Fail
History of the Eighties, Vol. 1, Chapter 7

facts.claim: The FDIC ultimately estimated its loss on the Continental Illinois assistance at about $1.1 billion, roughly 3 percent of the bank's assets at the time of the intervention.
facts.quote: the FDIC ultimately estimated its loss was about $1.1 billion, equal to about 3 percent of Continental's assets at the time of its intervention

facts.claim: In 1984 congressional hearings, Comptroller of the Currency C. T. Conover conceded that regulators lacked an effective way to handle the failure of the largest banks; commentators read his statement as applying to the eleven largest banks he had just discussed, and Representative Stewart McKinney responded with the phrase 'too big to fail'.
facts.quote: In congressional hearings, Comptroller C. T. Conover conceded that regulators lacked an effective way to handle a failure of the largest banks. Many commentators viewed Conover's statement as applying to the largest eleven banks that he had discussed just prior.

sources.title: History of the Eighties, Vol. 1, Chapter 7
The 1970s Origins of Too Big to Fail

openQuestions: The site says large depositors pulled 'more than $10 billion' in May 1984. Sources returned give more than $6 billion in the week to May 17 and about 30 percent of funding over ten days; the $10 billion figure may cover a longer period and should be checked against the FDIC chapter.

The site's '$4.5 billion' of FDIC assistance is consistent with the $1 billion capital infusion plus $3.5 billion of assumed debt, but no returned source states the $4.5 billion total; the FDIC chapter should be read for its own figure.

The site attributes the eleven-largest-banks remark to Conover's testimony; the FDIC chapter says commentators read his concession that way. The hearing transcript ('Inquiry into Continental Illinois Corp. and Continental Illinois National Bank', 98th Cong., 2d sess., 1984) is the primary record and was not retrieved.
No source returned described the role of chairman Roger Anderson in the bank's asset growth, as the site states.

The Cleveland Fed commentary notes that regulators had earlier bailed out Bank of the Commonwealth (1972) partly because it was viewed as too big to fail, so Continental was not the first such case; the site's 'birth of too big to fail' framing is contested.
